Name: budget_matched_query_formulation
Title: Does an LLM-Written Query Set Add Set Recall on a Keyword Scholarly-Search API Beyond a Deterministic Keyword Query at a Matched Result Budget?
Short Hypothesis: Does an LLM-written query set add at least 0.10 set recall on a keyword scholarly-search API beyond a deterministic keyword query set at a matched result budget? Although the recall gain of LLM-written queries over the verbatim question could come from shortening alone, an LLM-written query set exceeds a deterministic keyword query set by at least 0.10 set recall, which we conjecture is because the LLM supplies terms that are not in the question. This one contrast is tested, on the 597 LitSearch questions against OpenAlex with five queries and 25 results per query in both arms and small open models as the writer; the gain of keyword reduction over the verbatim question, the effect of query length and count, and run-to-run spread are only estimated. No simpler route answers it: term matching predicts only that shortening helps, and whether a model adds anything beyond the question's own words depends on what the search service returns, which no existing table records.
Related Work: Literature-search systems are compared by recall against annotated target papers, and live search engines are reported to perform poorly on natural-language literature questions: on 80 LitSearch questions Recall@5 is 17.5-62.5 for Google Search, Google Scholar and Elicit against 74.8 for a dense retriever (Ajith et al., 2024) [ajithetal2024]. In that probe the question was typed in verbatim, once, and five results were read, so the engine, the query form and the result budget are confounded. INSPIRE logs search-agent trajectories and finds that exposure is the largest observed loss (zero-exposure 17.4-56.1%), and states that its funnel is descriptive and that causal attribution needs intervention (Ding et al., 2026) [dingetal2026a]. RATIO shows that scores against a single mined positive understate retrieval quality, 24.5 against 41.2 MRR@10 when judge-accepted alternatives count (Sharon & Hope, 2026) [sharonhope2026]. LLM query expansion is reported to improve sparse and dense retrieval (Wang et al., 2023) [wangetal2023], on closed-corpus benchmarks with one expanded query (abstract only read); evidence synthesis evaluates human search strings by relative recall (Lagisz et al., 2025) [lagiszetal2025]. No retrieved paper compares query forms on a scholarly API with the number of queries and results held equal (lookup over all 358 retrieved records; titles and abstracts only, so a miss is weak evidence). Reported numbers used as the bar: BM25 50.0 and GritLM-7B 74.8 average Recall@5 on LitSearch specific questions [ajithetal2024]. Literature base: 205 screened-in papers, 19 read in full as plain-text conversions; arXiv and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited during the search, and the query-expansion papers were read as abstracts only.
Abstract: Literature-search systems are compared by recall against annotated target papers, and on that score live scholarly search is held to do poorly on natural-language questions. The comparison behind that belief typed each question in verbatim, issued it once and read five results, so it cannot say whether the search backend, the wording of the query or the number of results produced the score. The same confound sits inside every literature agent: when an agent that writes several queries finds more than a single verbatim query does, the gain may come from the model's knowledge, from mere shortening of an over-long query, or from the larger candidate set. Until these are separated, the loss of gold papers before ranking, which recent agent benchmarks identify as the largest one, cannot be assigned to a stage. We propose a within-question experiment on the 597 LitSearch questions against the OpenAlex search API in which three query-construction methods receive the same budget of five queries and 25 results each: the verbatim question, a deterministic keyword rule that uses only the question's own words, and a query set written by a small open language model with the first-stage prompt of an existing research pipeline. The primary test is the set-recall increment of the model-written queries over the deterministic rule, read against a threshold fixed in advance. An oracle title query gives the ceiling, keywords borrowed from another question give the floor that budget alone produces, and the contrast is repeated descriptively on TREC-COVID. We also estimate the gain of keyword reduction itself, the dependence on query length and count, and the spread over sampling seeds and API dates. The expected contribution is a budget-matched decomposition of where retrieval gain comes from, and a reproducible protocol for probing keyword search with questions.
Experiments: E0 [instrument] Data, identifiers and fixed rules. Download LitSearch (597 questions with specificity, source and gold S2ORC corpus ids; public; no human subjects; (licence unverified)) and its corpus titles and abstracts; resolve each gold id to an OpenAlex work (Semantic Scholar batch lookup for DOI / title, then OpenAlex by DOI, then title match at word overlap >= 0.85); questions with no resolved gold are listed and excluded. All HTTP responses go to a content-addressed cache keyed by method, URL and sorted parameters, so every later number is recomputable offline. Fix before any analysis: K = 5 queries and R = 25 results per query (the verbatim arm reads its first 125 results); the deterministic rule (lower-case, remove a fixed stop-word list, rank the question's remaining words by inverse document frequency over the LitSearch corpus; with w1..w6 the six highest-ranked words the five queries are {w1 w2 w3}, {w1 w2 w3 w4}, {w1 w2 w4}, {w1 w3 w5}, {w2 w3 w6}, each in question order, so the queries are not nested); the model arm (the harness's s1_init prompt verbatim, a small open instruct model of about 1.5B parameters downloaded from Hugging Face, about 3 GB, not cached, greedy decoding, JSON output; a parse failure counts as no results); the decision rule of E2. Decision rules are fixed before analysis in a git commit made before E2 runs; the commit hash is recorded in the results. Compute: download and id resolution about 30 min (estimated).

E1 [control C1] Positive control and ceiling. Query OpenAlex with the exact title of each gold paper, R = 25, and compute set recall (per question 1 if any gold is in the results). Expected at or above 0.95 on resolved questions; the value is the ceiling of every arm and separates 'not indexed or not returned by title' from query failure. Report the share and composition (inline-citation vs author-written, broad vs specific) of excluded questions. About 600 API calls (estimated).

E2 [tests C1] Budget-matched comparison. For each question issue the query set of each arm to OpenAlex works search (no year filter): VERB (the question as typed), DET (deterministic keyword query set), LLM (model-written query set). Set recall per question is 1 if any gold paper is in the union of the arm's results. Primary statistic: mean over questions of the difference LLM minus DET, with the two-sided 90% paired bootstrap interval over questions (10,000 resamples). Decision rule: the claim is supported if the lower limit is at or above 0.10 and refuted if the upper limit is below 0.10; otherwise undecided. With about 550 questions and a difference SD of 0.6, increments up to about 0.04 are refuted and increments from about 0.16 supported at 80% power; between them the design returns undecided, which is reported as such. Parse failures of the model are counted as no results and also reported separately, with the difference recomputed excluding them. Baselines for context: BM25 and dense-retriever Recall@5 on the closed LitSearch corpus as reported (LitSearch protocol as in [ajithetal2024]; not comparable in absolute terms because the index differs). About 6,600 API calls and one model pass over 597 questions, about 1.5 h on Apple MPS (estimated).

E3 [control C1] Negative control for the budget rival. Give each question the deterministic keyword query set of another question, same K and R, and compute set recall against the original question's gold, in two versions: (a) another LitSearch question (fixed derangement, seed recorded; same field, so a conservative floor) and (b) a TREC-COVID topic (unrelated field; a clean floor). Expected close to 0 for (b); a value above 0.05 would mean that a candidate set of this size contains gold papers whatever the wording, and E2 would then be reported net of it. About 6,000 API calls (estimated).

E4 [descriptive C2, C3] Where the gain comes from. (a) Estimate the set-recall gain of DET over VERB with a 95% paired bootstrap interval. (b) Set recall as a function of keywords per query (m = 2..6, one query) and of the number of queries (K = 1, 2, 5) for DET and LLM. (c) Diversity and overlap: unique results per arm, the E2 difference among questions where DET and LLM return a similar number of unique results (within 10%), the nested top-m rule (m = 2..6) as an additional deterministic arm, share of questions on which DET and LLM return identical result sets, Jaccard overlap of result sets, the difference of E2 recomputed outside identical sets, and the share of LLM query terms that are not words of the question. (d) Loss funnel per arm: gold not indexed, indexed but not returned by any query, returned. (e) Stratified by inline-citation vs author-written and broad vs specific questions. Uses cached responses plus about 5,000 calls (estimated).

E5 [descriptive C4] Noise floor and a second writer. Re-run the model arm with 3 sampling seeds at temperature 0.7 and report the range and standard deviation of set recall; re-issue all arms for a fixed random subset of 150 questions on a second date at least 7 days later (cache bypassed) and report the change; on the same subset run a second, larger open instruct model (about 3B parameters, about 6 GB download, not cached) and report its set recall beside the first model's. If recorded first-stage query sets of the deployed pipeline generator are supplied for the 80-question subset, score them as an additional arm at the same budget. About 5.5 h of model time (estimated).

E6 [descriptive C1] Second dataset. Repeat the three arms on the 50 TREC-COVID topics (question field as the natural-language need; public; no human subjects; (licence unverified)), adding the topics' human keyword query as a fourth arm. Because each topic has many judged-relevant documents, the outcome is the share of judged-relevant documents returned within the budget, matched to OpenAlex works by DOI or title. Report the paired LLM minus DET difference with a 95% bootstrap interval and whether its sign agrees with E2; no pass/fail rule, because the 0.10 threshold is defined on a 0/1 outcome. About 1,000 API calls and a download of about 100 MB (estimated).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Blind restatement unresolved: leakage - the model may have seen the gold papers and reproduce title words; data: LitSearch contains no question about a paper published after the training cut-off of the available open models and no post-cut-off question set is on this machine, so results are only stratified by question source.

Blind restatement unresolved: the outcome is coarse and gold-biased and questions with unresolved gold are excluded; data: LitSearch has no relevance labels beyond its annotated targets, and judging alternatives needs a human-validated LLM judge that is not available on this machine.

Blind restatement unresolved: external validity - one API with drifting results and one main dataset; data: keyless Semantic Scholar and arXiv search were rate-limited on this machine, and TREC-COVID's many-relevant structure does not admit the 0/1 threshold, so the second dataset carries no pass/fail rule.
Question narrowed from: How much does an LLM-written query set add to the set recall of a keyword scholarly-search API beyond a deterministic keyword query set at a matched result budget?
Rival not addressed - leakage: the model has seen the gold paper for a LitSearch question and writes its title words (primary claim).
Rival not addressed - bias: unlabelled relevant papers count as misses under single-gold recall (primary claim).

Power is marginal: no published effect size exists; against the 0.10 threshold the design separates true increments up to about 0.04 and from about 0.16 (SD 0.6, about 550 questions, one-sided 5%, 80% power), and returns undecided between them.

Scope: the writer is one or two small open instruct models, not the generator the pipeline deploys, and the comparator is one fixed deterministic rule; the result does not generalise to dense retrievers, web search engines, stronger generators or agents that revise queries after reading results.
The stated reason for an increment (terms not in the question) is a conjecture; term novelty is reported in E4 but no rule tests it.
Significance not supported by the literature: which stage of a literature agent should be changed first (third rung of the consequence ladder) rests on this study's reading of two papers.
The small model may write malformed queries, understating what an LLM adds; failures are reported separately.
OpenAlex may not index some gold papers and its results drift over time; the oracle query and the second-date re-query measure both.
Literature base: 19 of 205 papers read in full, as plain-text conversions; query-expansion work was read as abstracts only, so the novelty claim rests on titles and abstracts.
